modules.title: Lesson 1.1: Self & Identity (Ko)
modules.canDo: Introduce yourself and state your name or specific role using Ko.
modules.concept: 'Ko' introduces a specific identity—such as a proper name or a definite role ('the teacher'). The identity comes first, followed by the pronoun.

model.context: First greeting at a morning hui:
model.en: Hello! Who are you? — Hello! I am Mere.

check.question: Which word signals a specific name or identity at the start of the sentence?

prompts.situation: Introduce yourself as Mere:
Identify yourself as the teacher:

drills.explanation: 'Ko' marks specific identity before a name.

drills.instruction: Match the sentence to its pattern
drills.explanation: 'Ko' followed by a definite role and pronoun is the identity pattern.

modules.title: Lesson 1.2: Classifying Roles & Things (He)
modules.canDo: Describe what someone or something is ('a student', 'a worker') using He.
modules.concept: While 'Ko' names a specific person or 'the' role, 'He' classifies someone as 'a' member of a group (e.g. 'a student', 'a friend'). Notice 'te' is never used after 'He'.

model.en: I am a student. They are a teacher.

turns.speaker: Speaker B
turns.target: Āe, he tauira ahau. He kaiako ia.
turns.en: Yes, I am a student. They are a teacher.

check.question: Which sentence correctly says 'I am a student'?

prompts.situation: Tell a classmate that you are a student:
Introduce someone as a teacher:

drills.explanation: 'He' means 'a / an' and classifies a role without 'te'.
'tātou' means 'we (three or more, including the listener)'.
'He + noun + pronoun' classifies someone as a member of a category.

modules.title: Lesson 1.3: Origins & Homeland (Nō)
modules.canDo: Ask and state where you and others are from using Nō.
modules.concept: 'Nō' links a person to their home region, town, or country. Place names follow 'Nō' directly, followed by the pronoun.

model.context: Getting to know someone at a workshop:
model.en: Where are you from? — I am from Auckland.

check.question: Which particle asks or states a person's place of origin?

prompts.situation: Tell someone you are from Auckland:
Say that they are from Waikato:

drills.explanation: 'Ōtautahi' is the Māori name for Christchurch.
'hea' means 'where' — 'Nō hea koe?' asks where you are from.

drills.instruction: Match the sentence to its pattern
drills.explanation: 'Nō' states origin, whereas 'Kei' states current location.

modules.title: Lesson 2.1: Actions Happening Now (Kei te)
modules.canDo: Ask and describe what someone is doing right now using Kei te.
modules.concept: 'Kei te' places an ongoing action at the front of the clause, followed by the verb and then the person doing it.

model.en: What are you doing? — I am working.

check.question: Which marker shows the action is happening right now?

prompts.situation: Tell a colleague you are working:
Tell someone you are studying:
Say that they are reading:

drills.instruction: Match the sentence to its pattern
drills.explanation: 'Kei te + verb + pronoun' describes an action happening now.

modules.title: Lesson 2.2: Wellbeing & Feelings (Kei te)
modules.canDo: Ask how someone is feeling and describe your own wellbeing.
modules.concept: The same 'Kei te' frame works with descriptive state words like 'pai' (good), 'ngenge' (tired), or 'harikoa' (happy).

model.context: Greeting a friend in the morning:
model.en: How are you? — I am good, thank you.

turns.speaker: Speaker B
turns.target: Kei te pai ahau, kia ora!

check.question: How do you ask 'How are you?' in Te Reo Māori?

prompts.situation: Reply that you are feeling good:
Say that you are hungry:
Say that they are happy:

drills.instruction: Choose the question word for wellbeing
Match the sentence to its pattern
drills.explanation: 'Kei te + state + pronoun' describes how someone feels right now.

modules.title: Lesson 2.3: Past Actions (I)
modules.canDo: Describe actions that already happened using the past tense marker I.
modules.concept: Swap 'Kei te' for 'I' at the beginning of a verb clause to move the exact same sentence into the simple past tense—verbs themselves do not change form.

model.en: I walked yesterday. We ate together.

check.question: How do you change 'Kei te ako au' (I am studying) to 'I studied'?

prompts.situation: Say that you studied:
Say that you worked yesterday:

drills.explanation: 'I + verb + pronoun' places the action in the past.

modules.title: Lesson 3.1: Current Location (Kei)
modules.canDo: Ask and state where people and things are located right now using Kei.
modules.concept: 'Kei' followed by a place (like 'te tari' or 'konei') tells where someone is right now. Unlike 'Kei te + verb', here 'te' belongs to the place noun ('the office').

model.context: Texting a colleague before a meeting:
model.en: Where are you? — I am at the office.

check.question: How is 'Kei te tari au' (location) different from 'Kei te mahi au' (action)?

options.text: 'te tari' is a place ('the office'), while 'mahi' is a verb ('working')
They have the exact same meaning

prompts.situation: Tell a teammate you are at the office:
Say that they are at the house:

drills.instruction: Use the local place word (no "te" needed)
drills.explanation: Location words like 'konei' (here) follow 'Kei' directly without 'te'.

drills.instruction: Match the sentence to its pattern
drills.explanation: 'Kei + place + pronoun' states where someone is right now.

modules.title: Lesson 3.2: Relative Position (roto / waho / runga)
modules.canDo: Specify whether something is inside, outside, on top of, or underneath a landmark.
modules.concept: Position nouns ('roto' inside, 'waho' outside, 'runga' on/above, 'raro' under) follow 'Kei' directly and link to the landmark with 'i'.

model.context: Looking for a book in the office:
model.en: Where is the book? — On the desk.

check.question: Which small linking particle connects 'roto / runga' to the landmark?

prompts.situation: Say that it is on the desk:
Say that it is inside the house:

drills.explanation: 'i' links the spatial noun ('runga') to the landmark ('te tēpu').

drills.instruction: Match the sentence to its pattern
drills.explanation: Relative locations combine 'Kei + position + i + landmark'.

modules.title: Lesson 3.3: Movement & Direction (mai / atu)
modules.canDo: Give welcoming directions and describe movement towards or away from the speaker.
modules.concept: Directional particles follow the motion verb: 'mai' means towards the speaker ('come'), and 'atu' means away from the speaker ('go'). Use 'ki' for 'to / towards' a destination.

model.en: Come into the house! — Thank you, we are coming.
model.literal: [Go = Haere] + [Towards speaker = mai] + [To = ki] + [House = te whare]

turns.speaker: Speaker B
turns.target: Kia ora, kei te haere atu mātou.
turns.en: Thank you, we are heading over.

check.question: Which directional particle signals movement towards the speaker?

prompts.situation: Invite someone to the house:
Ask someone to come back here:

drills.instruction: Match the sentence to its pattern
drills.explanation: Motion verb + directional + 'ki' + destination directs movement.

modules.title: Lesson 4.1: Completed States (Kua)
modules.canDo: Announce when tasks are finished, ready, or underway using Kua.
modules.concept: 'Kua' signals that a change has taken place and a new state now holds—such as work being finished ('kua oti') or a meal being ready ('kua rite').

model.en: Is the work finished? — Yes, the work is finished!

check.question: Which marker announces that something has reached completion?

prompts.situation: Announce that the work is finished:
Call everyone because the food is ready:

drills.explanation: 'Kua' signals a completed transition into a new state.

drills.instruction: Match the sentence to its pattern
drills.explanation: 'Kua + state + subject' reports a completed result.

modules.title: Lesson 4.2: Suggestions & Obligations (Me)
modules.canDo: Make polite suggestions and state what should be done using Me.
modules.concept: 'Me' before a verb expresses 'should' or 'ought to'. It is widely used for collaborative suggestions like 'Me haere tātou' (We should go).

model.context: Deciding next steps with your group:
model.en: We should go now. — Yes, we should start.

turns.speaker: Speaker A
turns.target: Kua rite koe? Me haere tātou.
turns.en: Are you ready? We should go.

check.question: What does 'Me' communicate at the start of a verb sentence?

options.text: That an action should or ought to happen

prompts.situation: Suggest to the group that you should all go:
Advise someone that they should study:

drills.instruction: Match the sentence to its pattern
drills.explanation: 'Me + verb + pronoun' expresses polite obligation or advice.

pathways.label: Next: Lesson 4.3 (Connected Speech with nā te mea)

modules.title: Lesson 4.3: Explaining Why (nā te mea)
modules.canDo: Join two complete ideas to give a reason using nā te mea (because).
modules.concept: Combine any two patterns you have already learned by placing 'nā te mea' ('because') between them: e.g., action + 'nā te mea' + feeling or completed state.

model.context: Explaining why you are smiling at the end of the day:
model.en: I am happy because the work is finished.
model.target: Kei te harikoa au nā te mea kua oti te mahi.
model.literal: [I am happy] + [because = nā te mea] + [the work is finished]

turns.speaker: Speaker B
turns.target: Kei te harikoa au nā te mea kua oti te mahi.
turns.en: I am happy because the work is finished.

check.question: Which phrase joins a statement to its reason ('because')?

prompts.situation: Explain why you are eating:
prompts.target: I am eating because I am hungry.
expected: Kei te kai au nā te mea kei te hiakai au
Kei te kai ahau nā te mea kei te hiakai ahau

Kei te kai ahau nā te mea kei te hiakai au

prompts.situation: Explain why you are happy:
prompts.target: I am happy because the work is finished.
expected: Kei te harikoa au nā te mea kua oti te mahi
Kei te harikoa ahau nā te mea kua oti te mahi
prompts.hint: Kei te harikoa au + nā te mea + kua oti te mahi
